newsitem.title: USA: Stamp prices soar as serious collectors bid for rarities.
newsitem.headline: Stamp prices soar as serious collectors bid for rarities.

text.p: Stamp collecting may seem passe now that television provides far fuller pictures of distant places than a sticker on an envelope.
But as collectibles, stamps are hotter than ever before as serious collectors clamour for rare specimens, especially from the first 100 years of philately from 1840 to 1940.

"There may be smaller total numbers of collectors than there used to be, but the serious collectors at the top are stronger than they've ever been," said Norman Hubbard, chairman of Anphilex 1996, an exhibition billed as assembling the finest philatelic material ever in one place.

The exhibition over the Thanksgiving weekend at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel in New York will feature more than $100 million worth of stamps. The highlight is the Aristocrats of Philately -- 20 of the greatest individual stamps in the world.

Crowning the collection is an 1855 three-skilling Swedish colour error that fetched a record $2.3 million at an auction in Switzerland early this month. The stamp, which should have been green but turned out yellow, sold for $1.3 million in 1990 and was worth only $200,000 in 1971.

Two of the world's most important first-day covers, from Mauritius in 1848 and 1859, are now worth an estimated $3 million to $4 million each, versus $100,000 to $200,000 in 1971, when the last Anphilex exhibition was held.
The most valuable U.S. cover -- a 1851 Hawaiian issue with a two-cent stamp -- sold for $2.1 million at a New York auction in November 1995. In 1971, it could have been yours for just $150,000.

The appreciation of rare stamp values -- about 10 percent in the last 15 years -- has coincided with the decline of the leisurely hobby among the MTV generation, which is wowed by speedier pastimes in a computerized, shrinking world.

As governments issue innumerable stamps to boost revenues, diehard stamp collectors -- who are still believed to dwarf any other category of hobbyist -- have been forced to limit their purchases by subject or age.
"Serious collectors now pay no attention to new issues. They limit collecting to stamps issued perhaps 100 years ago or more," Hubbard said.

"At the other extreme, large numbers of cheap stamps appeal to kid collectors and small collectors. It's an entirely different world with its own dealers, parameters. The average collector is simply not a player any more when it comes to classic stamps."

The last stamp boom was in the 1970s, when a U.S. law allowed collectibles to be purchased for retirement accounts. Investors poured millions of dollars into stamps as a hedge against spiraling inflation, and widely traded issues became market barometers.

That all ended as inflation came under control in the early 1980s, and Congress repealed the law to encourage more conservative investments, said Tom Mazza, president of the Collectors Club in New York.

A former U.S. benchmark, the 1930 Zeppelin, which fetched $5,000 in the 1970s, is now worth about $1,000, said Colin Fraser, who heads Christie's stamp department. The 1929 British one-pound Postal Union Congress stamp, which peaked at about 2,000 pounds, or about $3,360 at today's exchange rate, in the 1970s is now valued at 250-300 pounds ($420 to $500) in mint condition. Another British bellwether, the 1930 one-pound Seahorse stamp has also tumbled since then from about 3,000 pounds ($5,040) to 350 pounds ($590).
But will new stamps -- especially "collectibles" featuring Elvis, James Dean and Marilyn Monroe from small, obscure countries -- be worth anything in the future?
"The potential for new stamps is zilch in my opinion," said Hubbard. "The average collector doesn't realise when he spends $25 on new issue, in most cases he can't even get $25 back."
Most stamps issued after 1950, he said, will fetch only about 60 percent to 70 percent of the face value, so it's better to just lick and stick them.

"Commercially, they're a bit of a dead loss" because there are just too many new issues, Fraser added. "But in terms of the overall market, they have an important role to fulfill" by attracting new collectors, he said.
If you want value, don't buy any stamp issued after 1940, Hubbard advises, even though there are exceptions.

"If you want a U.S. collection from 1900 to 1940, you could get a couple of hundred different stamps for a few hundred dollars, and have 80 percent of all stamps from that period," he said. "You will have something a lot more meaningful and which will hold a lot more value than new issues."
